input.question: How do hospitals dispose of donated blood/organs that go bad and can't be used anymore?
input.ground_truth: In some cases they don't. Back when I was a nuclear medicine intern I once saw an entire fridge filled with radioactive livers, some of which were many years old. The patients had been given radioactive medicine to help cure liver cancer, and in the cases when it didn't work and the patient died, they would have to remove the liver for safety reasons. Instead of spending the money to properly dispose of the radioactive waste (very expensive) the hospital just dumped them in an old fridge in the basement. This was at one of the top 10 hospitals in the US btw, not just some sketchy clinic.

Question: How do hospitals dispose of donated blood/organs that go bad and can't be used anymore?

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a juice box that you saved for later, but after a few days, it goes "yucky" and you can't drink it. Hospitals get blood and organs to help people who are sick, but sometimes those blood and organs can't be used because they get old or go "yucky" too.

When that happens, hospitals can't just throw them in the trash. They have to get rid of them in a very special way so nobody gets sick. Usually, they put them in special bags or containers and give them to companies that know how to make them safe again. Sometimes, the things that can't be used are heated up really, really hot or treated with special chemicals, so all the germs are gone. After that, they are thrown away in a safe way, just like how you throw away your yucky juice box, but even more careful! This keeps everyone safe and healthy.
